quals-wisconsin-algebra-2012s-01.title: Sylow theory and a permutation representation
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2012s-01.body:
**(a)** $n_{11}\equiv1\pmod{11}$ and $n_{11}\mid 392=2^3\cdot7^2$. The divisors of $392$ are $1,2,4,7,8,14,28,49,56,98,196,392$, and among them only $1$ and $56$ are $\equiv1\pmod{11}$. Let $Q\in\mathrm{Syl}_{11}(G)$; then $|N_G(Q)|=4312/n_{11}\in\{4312,77\}$, divisible by $7$ in either case. By Cauchy, $N_G(Q)$ has a subgroup $S$ of order $7$, and since $Q\trianglelefteq N_G(Q)$, $H=SQ$ is a subgroup of order $77$.

**(b)** In $H$ (order $77$), $n_7(H)\mid11$ with $n_7\equiv1\pmod 7$ gives $n_7(H)=1$, and $n_{11}(H)\mid7$ with $n_{11}\equiv 1\pmod{11}$ gives $n_{11}(H)=1$. So $H\cong C_7\times C_{11}$ is cyclic. Let $R\le H$ have order $7$. Choose a Sylow $7$-subgroup $P\ge R$ of $G$; $|P|=49$, so $P$ is abelian. Then $H$ and $P$ both centralize $R$, so $N_G(R)\supseteq C_G(R)\supseteq\langle H,P\rangle$, and $|N_G(R)|$ is divisible by $49$ and by $11$, i.e. by $539$. Hence $|G:N_G(R)|$ divides $4312/539=8$.

**(c)** Suppose $G$ is simple and let $k=|G:N_G(R)|$, $k\mid8$. If $k=1$ then $R\trianglelefteq G$ is a proper nontrivial normal subgroup — impossible. If $k\in\{2,4,8\}$, $G$ acts transitively on the $k$ cosets of $N_G(R)$; the kernel is a proper normal subgroup, hence trivial, so $G$ embeds in $S_k\le S_8$. Then $4312\mid8!=40320$, but $11\nmid 8!$ — contradiction. So $G$ is not simple. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2012s-02.title: Radicals of intersections
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2012s-02.body:
For finitely many ideals, $\sqrt{\bigcap X_i}=\bigcap\sqrt{X_i}$; and the radical of a primary ideal is prime.

**(a)** $\sqrt Q=\bigcap_i\sqrt{X_i}=\bigcap_iX_i=Q$, so $Q$ equals its radical, which is prime. Now $X_1X_2\cdots X_k\subseteq\bigcap X_i=Q$ with $Q$ prime, so $X_j\subseteq Q$ for some $j$ (if $x_i\in X_i\setminus Q$ for all $i$, then $x_1\cdots x_k\in Q$ contradicts primality). Since also $Q\subseteq X_j$, $Q=X_j$.

**(b)** Let $P_i=\sqrt{X_i}$ (prime) and $P=\sqrt Q=\bigcap_iP_i$ (prime). As in (a), $P\supseteq P_1\cdots P_k$ gives $P\supseteq P_j$ for some $j$; relabel so $j=1$. Since $P\subseteq P_i$ for all $i$, $P=P_1$, and for $i\ge2$, $P\subsetneq P_i$ because the radicals are distinct. (If $k=1$ there is nothing to prove.)

Claim: $\bigcap_{i\ge2}P_i\not\subseteq P$. Otherwise $P_2\cdots P_k\subseteq P$ and primality gives $P_i\subseteq P$ for some $i\ge2$, contradicting $P\subsetneq P_i$. Choose $s\in\bigcap_{i\ge2}P_i\setminus P$. For each $i\ge2$ some power of $s$ lies in $X_i$; taking $N$ large, $y=s^N\in Y=X_2\cap\cdots\cap X_k$, and $y\notin P$ as $P$ is prime.

Let $x\in X_1$. Then $xy\in X_1\cap Y=Q$, and no power of $y$ lies in $Q$ (since $y\notin P=\sqrt Q$). As $Q$ is primary, $x\in Q$. Hence $X_1\subseteq Q\subseteq X_1$, i.e. $Q=X_1$. (The Noetherian hypothesis is not needed.) ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2012s-03.title: Linear disjointness from $F$
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2012s-03.body:
**(a)** Let $g\in K[x]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $K$. Since $g(\alpha)=0$ and $g\in F[x]$, $f\mid g$ in $F[x]$. In a splitting field $\Omega$ of $f$ over $E$, write $f=\prod_i(x-\alpha_i)$; each $\alpha_i$ is a root of $g$, hence algebraic over $K$. The coefficients of $f$ are polynomial expressions in the $\alpha_i$, hence algebraic over $K$ (algebraic elements form a field). They lie in $F\subseteq E$ and are algebraic over $K$, so they lie in $F\cap A=K$.

**(b)** $B/K$ is finite and separable (characteristic $0$), so $B=K(\beta)$ by the primitive element theorem. Let $f$ be the monic minimal polynomial of $\beta$ over $F$. By (a), $f\in K[x]$; $f$ is irreducible over $F\supseteq K$, hence over $K$, and $f(\beta)=0$, so $f$ is also the minimal polynomial of $\beta$ over $K$. Therefore
$$[B:K]=\deg f=[F(\beta):F]\le[E:F].$$

**(c)** (Under the hypothesis of (b).) By (b), the degrees of finite subextensions of $A/K$ are bounded by $d=[E:F]$. Choose such a $B$ with $[B:K]$ as large as possible. For any $a\in A$, $B(a)$ is a finite extension of $K$ (as $a$ is algebraic) containing $B$, so $[B(a):K]\le[B:K]$ forces $B(a)=B$, i.e. $a\in B$. Hence $A=B$ and $[A:K]\le[E:F]$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2012s-04.title: Simultaneous triangularization
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2012s-04.body:
**(a)** Let $v\in E_\lambda(S)=\ker(S-\lambda I)$. Then $S(Tv)=T(Sv)=T(\lambda v)=\lambda\,Tv$, so $Tv\in E_\lambda(S)$.

**(b)** We prove, by induction on $k$: *pairwise commuting operators $A_1,\dots,A_k$ on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex space $W$ have a common eigenvector.* For $k=1$, the characteristic polynomial of $A_1$ has a root $\lambda\in\mathbb C$, giving an eigenvector. For $k\ge2$, let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $A_1$ and $W'=\ker(A_1-\lambda I)\ne0$. By (a), each $A_i$ maps $W'$ into itself, and the restrictions $A_2|_{W'},\dots,A_k|_{W'}$ commute pairwise. By induction they have a common eigenvector $w\in W'$; since $A_1w=\lambda w$, $w$ is a common eigenvector of all $A_i$. Apply this with $W=V$.

**(c)** Induction on $n=\dim V$; for $n=0$ take the trivial chain. Let $n\ge1$. By (b) there is a common eigenvector $v_1$; $V_1=\mathbb Cv_1$ is invariant under every $A_i$. Let $\pi\colon V\to\bar V=V/V_1$ and let $\bar A_i$ be the induced operators $\bar A_i(\pi v)=\pi(A_iv)$, well defined since $A_iV_1\subseteq V_1$; they commute pairwise. By induction ($\dim\bar V=n-1$) there is a chain $0=U_0\subseteq U_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq U_{n-1}=\bar V$ with $\dim U_j=j$ and $\bar A_iU_j\subseteq U_j$. Put $V_0=0$ and $V_j=\pi^{-1}(U_{j-1})$ for $1\le j\le n$. Then $\dim V_j=(j-1)+1=j$, the chain is nested with $V_1=\pi^{-1}(0)$ and $V_n=V$, and for $v\in V_j$, $\pi(A_iv)=\bar A_i\pi(v)\in U_{j-1}$, so $A_iv\in V_j$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2012s-05.title: Cayley–Hamilton in $GL(2,K)$
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2012s-05.body:
Since $-1$ is not a square, $-1\ne1$ (in characteristic $2$, $-1=1=1^2$), so $\operatorname{char}K\ne2$, and $x^2+1$ is irreducible over $K$.

**(a)** ($\Leftarrow$) By Cayley–Hamilton, $g^2-\mathrm{tr}(g)\,g+\det(g)I=0$, so $g^2=-I$. Then $g^4=I$ and $g^2=-I\ne I$, so $g$ has order $4$.

($\Rightarrow$) Let $g$ have order $4$ and let $m$ be its minimal polynomial; $\deg m\le2$ and $m\mid x^4-1=(x-1)(x+1)(x^2+1)$, a product of distinct irreducible factors. So $m$ is a product of some of these factors, of degree $\le2$: $m\in\{x-1,\ x+1,\ x^2-1,\ x^2+1\}$. In the first three cases $m\mid x^2-1$, so $g^2=I$, contradicting order $4$. Hence $m=x^2+1$. The characteristic polynomial is monic of degree $2$ and divisible by $m$, so it equals $x^2+1=x^2-\mathrm{tr}(g)x+\det(g)$. Thus $\mathrm{tr}(g)=0$ and $\det(g)=1$.

**(b)** $g=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has trace $0$ and determinant $1$, so it has order $4$ by (a) (indeed $g^2=-I$).

**(c)** Let $g$ be as in (b) and
$$h=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&-a\end{pmatrix},\qquad gh=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&-a\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-b&a\\a&b\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then $\mathrm{tr}(h)=0$, $\det h=-a^2-b^2=1$, and $\mathrm{tr}(gh)=0$, $\det(gh)=-b^2-a^2=1$. By (a), $g$, $h$ and $gh$ all have order $4$ (and lie in $G$, having determinant $1$). ∎
